John Maclean

By: Bernadette Maguire | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
From quadraplegic to disabled endurance sports star to walking again 25 years later - we retrace a life without limits.

Summary:
The tragic tackle which has left rising rugby league star Alex McKinnon with a broken neck and the prospect of never being able to walk again, is a sobering reminder of just how unforgiving spinal injuries can be.
John Maclean knows it better than anyone.
25 years ago, he too was an up and coming footy player when he was struck down in the cruelest of ways.
While on a training ride on Sydney's M4 motorway, a truck smashed into John, leaving him paralysed from the waist down.
Not that life in a wheelchair has held him back.
He's since achieved the most incredible feats - from swimming the English Channel to finishing the Hawaiian ironman.
But John has never given up hope of walking again.
Now, John's achieving things that are astounding the medical world and redefining what might be possible for people with spinal injuries.

There is inspiring video that charts the course of John's career from disabled athlete to those first few tentative ragdoll steps to walking again.

We have been offered an exclusive with John Maclean and have access to any venue of our choice at The Campus.

WE ALSO HAVE ACCESS TO ALL THE RAW FOOTAGE USED TO PRODUCE THE VIDEOS ON JOHN'S LIFE - ALL THE SPORTS EVENTS, HIS THERAPY, FIRST TENTATIVE STEPS ON THE BEACH. REMARKABLE INSPIRING MATERIAL.

Further information:
Since he was a little boy looking out the window of his classroom in Western Sydney, the soon-to-be 47-year-old (May 27) John Maclean has dreamed of being an athlete and playing professional rugby.

By the time Maclean reached the age of 22, he was a reserve-grade player for the precursor to the Australian National Rugby League – the New South Wales Rugby League, as well a burgeoning triathlete.
Those dreams were thought to have been shattered on June 27, 1988, when Maclean was struck from behind by an eight-ton truck while on the road training for the upcoming Nepean Triathlon on his bicycle. The collision left Maclean with a broken back, pelvis and right arm. From that moment on, Maclean was rendered a paraplegic.
That is where this story begins.
From a moment in time when some would give up and fall, Maclean picked himself up – again, and again, and again. His determination undaunted, his resolve unwavering and his competitive fire burning more intense than ever, Maclean began to train, to compete, to win.
His first stop was a return to Nepean in 1994 where he became Australia’s first paraplegic triathlete. He then became the first person in a wheelchair to complete the Ironman World Championship in Kona, and the first to swim the treacherous English Channel — not once, but twice (1995, 1998). He even trained with the national wheelchair basketball team in 1995 as they prepared for the 1996 Atlanta Olympics


The first non-US citizen and first paraplegic athlete to be inducted into the Ironman Hall of Fame returned to Kona twice more in back-to-back years (1996-97) and became the first paraplegic to complete the course before the cut-off time for able-bodied competitors in the latter year.
He has participated in the Sydney to Hobart Yacht Race, took part in the Ultraman endurance challenge, and Maclean even represented his country at both the Olympic Games and Paralympics in 2000 before winning a silver medal in rowing at the 2008 Beijing Paralympics.
Winner of the Order of Australia Medal for his service to sport as a triathlete and swimmer, Maclean is the first Australian person to participate in an Olympic, Paralympic or world championship competition in five separate sports. He has been immortalised in film and in books, and has starred alongside global sporting icons Muhammad Ali, Michael Jordan, Tiger Woods, Usain Bolt and Nadia Comaneci in a 2008 Super Bowl advertisement for Gatorade.
“I thought a door had closed, but in actual fact all it did was open a different door as a wheelchair athlete,” Maclean told TriRadar. “Now there is an opportunity to get back to where I used to be which is the ultimate dream.”
The ultimate dream Maclean speaks of is finishing what he started — to race Nepean, Australia’s oldest continuing triathlon — out of the wheelchair and on his own two feet. With the help of Neurophysicist Ken Ware, founder of Neurotricional Sciences, whom he met through mutual friend and 2012 Ironman World Champion Pete Jacobs, Maclean is now walking.
“John’s progress is nothing out of the ordinary in regards to Ken’s treatment,” said Jacobs, who had sought treatment from Ware himself to alleviate nagging hip pain. “Ken sees responses daily that lead to the type of progress John has had. John sets very big goals and is very clearly driven to those goals with motivation and focus that few have and that has sped up his overall progress.”
Jacobs explained to TriRadar that within days of seeing Ware, he had learned a lot about the body through Ware’s teachings and also completely removed the pain through his treatment.
“I understood this treatment could help John with his constant pain, his shoulder problem, and possibly help him walk again,” said Jacobs. “It was just good timing that John was visiting Noosa just after I’d seen Ken and I was able to convince John that this really does work despite sounding completely out of the box and unheard of.”
According to Jacobs, that while Ware treats all patients the same since everybody has the same underlying makeup, John’s was slightly different.
“John became a special case because of his circumstances, being a partial paraplegic, which meant some signals were able to get through and Ken was able to exploit those small pathways and create new, much larger ones relatively quickly, which meant obvious results, quickly,” he said. “There is no doubt John will complete this goal. He is an amazingly talented and strong individual, and he will keep progressing with his abilities between now and then.”
For Maclean founder of the John Maclean Foundation, which assists wheelchair users under the age of 18, Jacobs’ introduction to Ware has opened the door to a world of further possibilities and adventures.

“I’m really excited and thankful to Pete, as the one guy that made this happen is Ken Ware,” said Maclean. “He got me to think differently and act differently and it all created a different result. By using his ‘Ware K Tremor’ therapy I have been given a second chance and it’s my intention to finish what I started and complete the Nepean on my feet.
So, on October 26, a full 26 years after the incident that almost left him wheelchair-bound for the rest of his life, Maclean will set out to complete the 1km swim, 30km bike ride and 10km run.
“I should have been dead 26 years ago,” said Maclean. ”So, I am trying to make the most out of life for not just me, but all of us.
“I have a new bike from the guys at Panther Cycles in Penrith with components from Shimano, and I covered half the distance on the bike in training which has been a challenge,” he said. “I have covered almost half the distance walking, but I believe in my mind I can do it. I feel that I can do it today.
“I don’t see myself as being any different than anyone else. I’ve always wanted to be seen as an equal, but the biggest joy in life is having balance. Giving back to my family, giving back to the community, accepting new challenges and meeting new friends, and most importantly, being able to literally pick my son up from school. That’s how I judge whether or not my life is successful.
“Life is amazing,” he concluded. “It’s like an ice cream store with thousands of flavours and I want to try each and every one.”

His ability to walk again is thanks to a grounbreaking therapy pioneered by Ken Ware 20 odd years ago,

Researchers around the world are extensively studying the role that ‘Chaos’ plays in our physical and emotional health and wellbeing. Chaos, Nonlinear Dynamics and Complexity, attracts significant attention in many fields -such as sociology, physics, biology and engineering. The research primarily focuses on applications in neural networks, biological and social systems, secure communications and information science. We introduce a dynamical, ‘self initiated’ novel therapy, that exploits the natural chaotic rhythms of the human nervous system. The therapy has been successfully utilized for more than 25 years*, to assist patients with often critical disorders, regain control over their physical/emotional health and wellness futures. The ‘present day’ clients highlighted in this presentation, have overcome long term debilitating neurological restraints/conditions within very small (unprecedented) time scales. Accomplishments such as these are representative of programing and reprogramming/plasticity, recalibrating the central nervous system on a global scale, positively affecting all of the systems sub systems simultaneously. We have utilized EMG, EEG, and ECG simultaneously to observe these positive global transitions to the therapy. Whilst these data provides substantial evidence of enhanced neurological complexity, the real data are in the positive results that the clients obtain from this unique therapy. This poster/video presentation will propose the mechanisms at work relating to the success of the therapy and emphasize the significance of ‘arousal control’ by the Clients to optimize reprograming, reprograming/plasticity potential; while they initiate the prescribed, very slow mild resistance exercises, in a super relaxed state. A ‘self organizing’ chaotic tremor emerges that evolves over time, rapidly enhancing the systems complexity – Programming and Reprogramming and/or Reorganizing the Central Nervous System . The re-established or enhanced neurological complexity of the system, enables the client to perform desirable physical tasks that had previously been thought of as impossible; not likely to be accomplished because of lesion; or dramatically impaired. Most commonly, long term attempt to acquire same through all other forms of therapy have failed. .* It must be noted that the significant positive effects of this therapy were accidentally discovered more than 25 years ago by Ken Ware. Clients attending the original centre (The Pioneer Valley Hospital in Mackay, Queensland Australia) were significantly benefiting from these techniques long before we had a scientific framework to begin to explain how the therapy worked. This will remain a work in progress.
he pair embarked on sessions of “Ware K Tremor” therapy — an unusual treatment which saw Maclean flaying around like a rag doll as part of a process to recalibrate his nervous system.
He then started to take his first faltering steps in more than 20 years.
“He believes it can unlock the nervous system to access things it wouldn’t do before,’’ Maclean said.
Maclean said he has always believed he could do anything in life. But even he never believed he would be able to walk again. Maclean said.

Press Release:


Live without Limits
25 years ago, while out on a training ride, a truck crashed into athlete Jon Maclean, leaving him paralysed from the waist down. He went on to achieve the unthinkable, from swimming the English Channel and completing the Hawaiian Ironman to participating in the Olympics and Paralympics. John never thought he would walk again. Carte Blanche meets an athlete back on his feet and astounding the medical world by redefining the possibilities for people with spinal injuries.


Script:


Live Without Limits

Lose 3 sec VO: 8”
All John Maclean ever wanted to be was a professional athlete…by 1988 he was playing professional rugby for the Warragamba Wombats.

Upsound…

John Maclean has also represented SG Ball and Jersey…


John:

I was a young guy who had the world at his feet, I was doing well and playing football and sports and I couldn’t imagine a better life for me at that stage.


VO: 10”
But then fate played a devastating hand…as John was cycling down the highway training for his first triathlon – an 8 ton truck ploughed into him.

John:
I’d broken my back in 3 places, my pelvis in 4 places, my right arm in 2 places, fractured sternum, broken ribs, I’d broken 16 bones.

Derek:
You know John at what stage do you really decide to live?

John:
I felt that there was a time that I had a choice of leaving or staying, and maybe that was induced by the morphine…but I vividly recall saying to myself that I don’t want to die.

VO: 5”
John was left an incomplete paraplegic with only 25% use of his left leg.

John:
There was a cathartic moment with my Dad and I had a cry and my Dad gave me a cuddle and he said those famous words, “Son how far can you go,” and that’s when I shifted trying to walk and asked what can I do as a person using a wheelchair.

Link
Ironically the first event that John competed in was the Nepean triathlon, the event that he had been training for on that fateful day a few years earlier.

John:
It was huge for me to go back with my best friend John Young, to ride past where I got hit by the truck, to finally cross the finish line was quite special…which then led on to other things.

shorter VO:
Sport became his way to prove he was equal.

John:
I really struggled going from a professional footballer signing autographs for kids to this label that I had a disability and was handicapped and I really struggled that my life was so different post the injury, so I thought if I could do that, my life would be different.

Link Hawaii Ironman
But the triathlon was just the start. John happened to be watching the ultra demanding Hawaii ironman on TV and suddenly he had a new goal.

John:
And I thought I’d like to be the first in the world to take that on and again to be seen as equal. That’s a very big mountain now, that’s an Everest.

Derek:
The day dawns after all that training, how are you feeling?

John:
You know I dreamed about this life as an athlete and now it had presented as a wheelchair athlete on the world’s biggest stage for ironman.

Upsound
Amazingly not too far off the pace the professionals are setting John Maclean pulls himself through the water…

VO:
John navigated his way through the throngs in the 3.8km swim, but it was the gruelling 180km hand cycle on unforgiving hills in searing heat that nearly beat him.

John:
The hill was that steep that the front wheel started to lift off the ground and I thought to myself that is the end of the day. And one of my friends said to me, turn the wheelchair around backwards and pull yourself up the first hill.

VO:
He missed the cycle cutoff time by 40 minutes but the organisers allowed him to continue.

John:
Then I start my first ever marathon and clearly I was tired to begin with and then one of the hills going up backwards I looked at Johhno and I said I was tired aand he said the pain won’t last forever but the memories will which then inspired me to get to the finish line.

VO:
John trained harder the following year – and he would have made the cycle cutoff if it wasn’t for a blowout on his bike. In 1997 he was joined by two other wheelchair athletes – the pressure was on, but he was third time lucky.

John:
It was so rewarding to finally cross the finish line in 1997, receiving the finishers medal and winning the category.

VO:
A victory that later saw him inducted into the Ironman hall of fame. John didn’t stop there – he was eyeing the English channel.

Lose link
John:
And then I found out that no athlete, athlete full stop had ever completed the Hawaii Ironman and swum the English channel and I wanted to be the first.

VO:
He put on 20 kilos and made his first attempt at crossing in August 1998.

John:
The best way to share that experience with viewers is to imagine getting into your bathtub, fill up your bathtub with cold water, add ice, some salt, then place the bathtub on a roller coaster and make the roller coaster go quite fast.

VO:
After 9 hours the tide was against him – he struggled for a further 3 hours before the captain pulled the plug.

John:
I was devastated but I understood in that process that mother nature runs the race not individuals.

VO:
13 days later he made a second attempt – this time conditions were kinder.

John:
Round about 12 hours the captain of the boat said you need to pick it up now because if you miss this tidal change you will miss the land altogether. So you can imagine after twelve hours of swimming and someone now telling you to lift your game, its not as if I wasn’t already lifting my game, so I’m lucky that I tried as hard as I could and gave it everything I could and eventually got over that last tidal change and managed to land 12 hours and 55, quite relieved.

VO:
He bummed his way up the beach – exhausted.

Upsound

Sometimes you win and sometimes you lose but today hopefully I’ve won for all those little boys and girls in wheelchairs who need someone to look up to, hopefully they have got someone to do that now.

VO:
John was unstoppable. In 2000 he represented the Australia in Sydney Olympics, in 2001 he crewed for the Sydney to Hobart race. In 2005 he was the first wheelchair athlete to complete the grueling Molakai challenge. Then in 2008 he announced he’d be retiring from professional sport after his last event – adaptive rowing at the Beijing Olympics with team mate Kathryn Ross.

John:

Up to the finish line China, Australia, China, Australia so I knew it was going to be very close and it ended up being very close.

Upsound
China, Australia, China, Australia, Australia making a last attempt but its going to be China though.

John:
Beaten by less than one second.

Upsound:
What a wonderful row!

VO:
Then another door opened – John was introduced to Ken Ware, who had developed what he called tremor therapy. It’s a combination of neurology, physics and physiotherapy.

Derek:
You talk about getting rid of nervous noise in the body?

Ken:
Yes, basically the underlying state of our nervous system are chaotic as opposed to our idea that everything is nice and stable down there.

VO:
The induced tremors release past trauma, making way for nerve regeneration.

John:
What happens over time is that it illicits this tremor and Ken would say let it all go, let go, let go and then you are in this space of being really present and then what happens over time is it builds up this velocity and then your arms start shaking and you go into this tremor. Remembering your eyes are closed and then he would say, okay its time to let it migrate through your body and so the tremor is not just in my upper body its coming down into my legs.

VO:
Given that John’s spinal cord wasn’t completely severed Ken was optimistic.
John:
After a series of these exercises Ken then asked what is it that you want to do and I then very clearly and articulately said “I want to walk and he said you should be able to do that.”

VO:
Just 3 days later he attempted his first unaided steps.

John:
And then he said close your eyes and try to walk and it took everything neutrally to not fall over and then eventually after taking 15 steps he said now open your eyes and walk. And then not in the way that you would walk, but I was able to walk after all these years just by letting go of everything that has held me back.

VO:
John had always wanted to walk on the beach with his wife.

Ken:
We stood on the waters edge for a little bit and let his system calibrate to what we call pink noise which is the sound of the ocean and the wind, letting his sensory awareness take notice of those things and as that was taking place I was watching his feet how they were fine tuning to are re-adjusting to the changes that were taking place as the water went to and fro through his feet.

VO:
Then he drew a line in the sand.

Ken
I said no no I just want you to sprint, I just want to see what happens, so he took off and after three or 4 steps and fell flat on his face in the sand.

VO:
A few adjustments and John tasted freedom.

Ken:
The next minute he was flatout down the beach and he got about 50 metres and we stopped and had a laugh and a cuddle and that’s when he and Amanda walked back holding hands.

John:
And to walk with my wife on the beach, which again I had not done for such a long time, that was a special moment.

VO:
26 years after the accident John found himself signing up for the Nepean triathlon again – this time as an able bodied athlete. The swim and cycle was easy going, but it was the 10km walk in carbon fibre leg braces that was nearly his undoing.

John:
The pain that was associated with having these carbon fibre leg braces to take again one step at a time. On the second lap Darren the guy who designed the leg braces had to take them off and my feet were covered in blood, the skin had been ripped right off.

VO:
Despite the pain giving up wasn’t an option.

John:
I think I was crying for the last 5km to eventually have the opportunity to cross the finish line, so much pain.

VO:
He was the last man in, but he’d come full circle.

John:
My wife was there every step of the way, our son joined us for the last little bit and we held hands and we crossed the finish line together and that was my absolute highlight crossing that line with my wife and my son.

VO;
Nowadays he spends his time inspiring people around the world as a global brand ambassador... His message…see only possibilities. His story challenges us all to ask how far can we go?

John:
How far can we all go? How does that look like for you and the people you care about? If you can learn to let go of the past then you can embrace the present and the future because we are all held back by the past.

Promo 10”

Paraplegic John Maclean was the first athlete to complete both the grueling Hawaii Ironman and crossing the English channel…challenging us all to ask – how far can you go?

Promo 15”

VO: 5”
Can a paraplegic learn to walk again? And even compete in a triathlon?

John:
Tears streaming down face last 5 km…

VO: 4”
Meet John Maclean a wheelchair athlete who has come full circle.


Promo 15”

VO: 9”

His dreams of becoming a professional athlete were dashed when he was hit by a truck leaving him a paraplegic. But there was no stopping John Maclean.

John:
Hawaii Ironman…and English channel.

Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 04 June 2015 Press Release: Live without Limits 25 years ago, while out on a training ride, a truck crashed into athlete Jon Maclean, leaving him paralysed from the waist down. He went on to achieve the unthinkable, from swimming the English Channel and completing the Hawaiian Ironman to participating in the Olympics and Paralympics. John never thought he would walk again. Carte Blanche meets an athlete back on his feet and astounding the medical world by redefining the possibilities for people with spinal injuries. Script: Live Without Limits Lose 3 sec VO: 8” All John Maclean ever wanted to be was a professional athlete…by 1988 he was playing professional rugby for the Warragamba Wombats. Upsound… John Maclean has also represented SG Ball and Jersey… John: I was a young guy who had the world at his feet, I was doing well and playing football and sports and I couldn’t imagine a better life for me at that stage. VO: 10” But then fate played a devastating hand…as John was cycling down the highway training for his first triathlon – an 8 ton truck ploughed into him. John: I’d broken my back in 3 places, my pelvis in 4 places, my right arm in 2 places, fractured sternum, broken ribs, I’d broken 16 bones. Derek: You know John at what stage do you really decide to live? John: I felt that there was a time that I had a choice of leaving or staying, and maybe that was induced by the morphine…but I vividly recall saying to myself that I don’t want to die. VO: 5” John was left an incomplete paraplegic with only 25% use of his left leg. John: There was a cathartic moment with my Dad and I had a cry and my Dad gave me a cuddle and he said those famous words, “Son how far can you go,” and that’s when I shifted trying to walk and asked what can I do as a person using a wheelchair. Link Ironically the first event that John competed in was the Nepean triathlon, the event that he had been training for on that fateful day a few years earlier. John: It was huge for me to go back with my best friend John Young, to ride past where I got hit by the truck, to finally cross the finish line was quite special…which then led on to other things. shorter VO: Sport became his way to prove he was equal. John: I really struggled going from a professional footballer signing autographs for kids to this label that I had a disability and was handicapped and I really struggled that my life was so different post the injury, so I thought if I could do that, my life would be different. Link Hawaii Ironman But the triathlon was just the start. John happened to be watching the ultra demanding Hawaii ironman on TV and suddenly he had a new goal. John: And I thought I’d like to be the first in the world to take that on and again to be seen as equal. That’s a very big mountain now, that’s an Everest. Derek: The day dawns after all that training, how are you feeling? John: You know I dreamed about this life as an athlete and now it had presented as a wheelchair athlete on the world’s biggest stage for ironman. Upsound Amazingly not too far off the pace the professionals are setting John Maclean pulls himself through the water… VO: John navigated his way through the throngs in the 3.8km swim, but it was the gruelling 180km hand cycle on unforgiving hills in searing heat that nearly beat him. John: The hill was that steep that the front wheel started to lift off the ground and I thought to myself that is the end of the day. And one of my friends said to me, turn the wheelchair around backwards and pull yourself up the first hill. VO: He missed the cycle cutoff time by 40 minutes but the organisers allowed him to continue. John: Then I start my first ever marathon and clearly I was tired to begin with and then one of the hills going up backwards I looked at Johhno and I said I was tired aand he said the pain won’t last forever but the memories will which then inspired me to get to the finish line. VO: John trained harder the following year – and he would have made the cycle cutoff if it wasn’t for a blowout on his bike. In 1997 he was joined by two other wheelchair athletes – the pressure was on, but he was third time lucky. John: It was so rewarding to finally cross the finish line in 1997, receiving the finishers medal and winning the category. VO: A victory that later saw him inducted into the Ironman hall of fame. John didn’t stop there – he was eyeing the English channel. Lose link John: And then I found out that no athlete, athlete full stop had ever completed the Hawaii Ironman and swum the English channel and I wanted to be the first. VO: He put on 20 kilos and made his first attempt at crossing in August 1998. John: The best way to share that experience with viewers is to imagine getting into your bathtub, fill up your bathtub with cold water, add ice, some salt, then place the bathtub on a roller coaster and make the roller coaster go quite fast. VO: After 9 hours the tide was against him – he struggled for a further 3 hours before the captain pulled the plug. John: I was devastated but I understood in that process that mother nature runs the race not individuals. VO: 13 days later he made a second attempt – this time conditions were kinder. John: Round about 12 hours the captain of the boat said you need to pick it up now because if you miss this tidal change you will miss the land altogether. So you can imagine after twelve hours of swimming and someone now telling you to lift your game, its not as if I wasn’t already lifting my game, so I’m lucky that I tried as hard as I could and gave it everything I could and eventually got over that last tidal change and managed to land 12 hours and 55, quite relieved. VO: He bummed his way up the beach – exhausted. Upsound Sometimes you win and sometimes you lose but today hopefully I’ve won for all those little boys and girls in wheelchairs who need someone to look up to, hopefully they have got someone to do that now. VO: John was unstoppable. In 2000 he represented the Australia in Sydney Olympics, in 2001 he crewed for the Sydney to Hobart race. In 2005 he was the first wheelchair athlete to complete the grueling Molakai challenge. Then in 2008 he announced he’d be retiring from professional sport after his last event – adaptive rowing at the Beijing Olympics with team mate Kathryn Ross. John: Up to the finish line China, Australia, China, Australia so I knew it was going to be very close and it ended up being very close. Upsound China, Australia, China, Australia, Australia making a last attempt but its going to be China though. John: Beaten by less than one second. Upsound: What a wonderful row! VO: Then another door opened – John was introduced to Ken Ware, who had developed what he called tremor therapy. It’s a combination of neurology, physics and physiotherapy. Derek: You talk about getting rid of nervous noise in the body? Ken: Yes, basically the underlying state of our nervous system are chaotic as opposed to our idea that everything is nice and stable down there. VO: The induced tremors release past trauma, making way for nerve regeneration. John: What happens over time is that it illicits this tremor and Ken would say let it all go, let go, let go and then you are in this space of being really present and then what happens over time is it builds up this velocity and then your arms start shaking and you go into this tremor. Remembering your eyes are closed and then he would say, okay its time to let it migrate through your body and so the tremor is not just in my upper body its coming down into my legs. VO: Given that John’s spinal cord wasn’t completely severed Ken was optimistic. John: After a series of these exercises Ken then asked what is it that you want to do and I then very clearly and articulately said “I want to walk and he said you should be able to do that.” VO: Just 3 days later he attempted his first unaided steps. John: And then he said close your eyes and try to walk and it took everything neutrally to not fall over and then eventually after taking 15 steps he said now open your eyes and walk. And then not in the way that you would walk, but I was able to walk after all these years just by letting go of everything that has held me back. VO: John had always wanted to walk on the beach with his wife. Ken: We stood on the waters edge for a little bit and let his system calibrate to what we call pink noise which is the sound of the ocean and the wind, letting his sensory awareness take notice of those things and as that was taking place I was watching his feet how they were fine tuning to are re-adjusting to the changes that were taking place as the water went to and fro through his feet. VO: Then he drew a line in the sand. Ken I said no no I just want you to sprint, I just want to see what happens, so he took off and after three or 4 steps and fell flat on his face in the sand. VO: A few adjustments and John tasted freedom. Ken: The next minute he was flatout down the beach and he got about 50 metres and we stopped and had a laugh and a cuddle and that’s when he and Amanda walked back holding hands. John: And to walk with my wife on the beach, which again I had not done for such a long time, that was a special moment. VO: 26 years after the accident John found himself signing up for the Nepean triathlon again – this time as an able bodied athlete. The swim and cycle was easy going, but it was the 10km walk in carbon fibre leg braces that was nearly his undoing. John: The pain that was associated with having these carbon fibre leg braces to take again one step at a time. On the second lap Darren the guy who designed the leg braces had to take them off and my feet were covered in blood, the skin had been ripped right off. VO: Despite the pain giving up wasn’t an option. John: I think I was crying for the last 5km to eventually have the opportunity to cross the finish line, so much pain. VO: He was the last man in, but he’d come full circle. John: My wife was there every step of the way, our son joined us for the last little bit and we held hands and we crossed the finish line together and that was my absolute highlight crossing that line with my wife and my son. VO; Nowadays he spends his time inspiring people around the world as a global brand ambassador... His message…see only possibilities. His story challenges us all to ask how far can we go? John: How far can we all go? How does that look like for you and the people you care about? If you can learn to let go of the past then you can embrace the present and the future because we are all held back by the past. Promo 10” Paraplegic John Maclean was the first athlete to complete both the grueling Hawaii Ironman and crossing the English channel…challenging us all to ask – how far can you go? Promo 15” VO: 5” Can a paraplegic learn to walk again? And even compete in a triathlon? John: Tears streaming down face last 5 km… VO: 4” Meet John Maclean a wheelchair athlete who has come full circle. Promo 15” VO: 9” His dreams of becoming a professional athlete were dashed when he was hit by a truck leaving him a paraplegic. But there was no stopping John Maclean. John: Hawaii Ironman…and English channel.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): From quadraplegic to disabled endurance sports star to walking again 25 years later - we retrace a life without limits.
metadata.Summary: The tragic tackle which has left rising rugby league star Alex McKinnon with a broken neck and the prospect of never being able to walk again, is a sobering reminder of just how unforgiving spinal injuries can be. John Maclean knows it better than anyone. 25 years ago, he too was an up and coming footy player when he was struck down in the cruelest of ways. While on a training ride on Sydney's M4 motorway, a truck smashed into John, leaving him paralysed from the waist down. Not that life in a wheelchair has held him back. He's since achieved the most incredible feats - from swimming the English Channel to finishing the Hawaiian ironman. But John has never given up hope of walking again. Now, John's achieving things that are astounding the medical world and redefining what might be possible for people with spinal injuries. There is inspiring video that charts the course of John's career from disabled athlete to those first few tentative ragdoll steps to walking again. We have been offered an exclusive with John Maclean and have access to any venue of our choice at The Campus. WE ALSO HAVE ACCESS TO ALL THE RAW FOOTAGE USED TO PRODUCE THE VIDEOS ON JOHN'S LIFE - ALL THE SPORTS EVENTS, HIS THERAPY, FIRST TENTATIVE STEPS ON THE BEACH. REMARKABLE INSPIRING MATERIAL.
